verses.note: In its first setting the verse declared a human king God's son by adoption on the day of his crowning. The New Testament applies it to Jesus at his baptism, his resurrection, and his exaltation, and the church confessed that the one so declared is the eternal Son, whose sonship the royal adoption only foreshadowed.

Whatever the first singer intended, the verse holds together two things the church would later confess of Christ: the one addressed is called God, and in the next breath God is his God who anoints him. Hebrews reads that tension as the relation of the eternal Son to the Father, a relation the creeds of Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451) set in words.

The child's name says what the sign is: God with us. Isaiah's first readers heard it as a promise that God would be present to save Judah. The New Testament hears it as a statement of who Jesus is, God come to be with his people in human flesh, and Matthew frames his Gospel with it (Matthew 1:23, 28:20).

A child is born and a son is given: Christian interpreters have long heard in the pair both the human birth and the divine gift, the one who is truly a child of a human mother and the Son sent from God (Galatians 4:4). The title Mighty God, on the same child, is one of the Old Testament's strongest witnesses to the confession that the Messiah is God come among us.

The Servant comes without the appearance of power, from unpromising ground. The Gospels' account of Jesus from Nazareth, a village that prompted the question whether anything good could come from it (John 1:46), matches this picture of a root in dry ground. God's saving arm arrives in ordinary, even unattractive, human form.

The Christological reading of Jerome and much of the medieval church saw here the virgin conception of Christ. Most modern interpreters, Catholic and Protestant, do not think the Hebrew requires or intends that, and the New Testament never cites the verse. It remains part of the church's history of reading, not a proof text for the doctrine, which rests on Matthew 1 and Luke 1.

Christians have read the ruler's ‘origins... from the days of eternity’ alongside his birth in Bethlehem as a pairing of eternal origin and human birth. The Hebrew phrase can mean the remote past, so the verse is a support for the doctrine rather than its proof; the doctrine itself rests on texts such as John 1:1-14.

God speaks of himself as the one pierced and then of ‘him’ for whom they mourn. Christians have seen in this shift a glimpse of one who is identified with God and yet distinct, pierced in a human body, a reading made possible, though not proven, by the text's own grammar.

The verse places Jesus in the royal line through Joseph while declining to call Joseph his father. It is the genealogy's own way of saying what the church later confessed: Jesus is truly a son of Israel and of David, and his origin is not simply from them.

The verse states the conception without a human father as fact and without explanation. The church's confession that the Son was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary rests on this verse and Luke 1:35.

Matthew translates the name so that no reader will miss it: God with us. Set beside the conception by the Spirit, the name is the Gospel's first statement that in Jesus God himself has come to be present with his people, and it frames the book with the promise of 28:20.

The verse keeps both halves of Matthew's claim together: Jesus was born of a woman who had not known a man, and he was received into a human family and given a name by a human father. The Son of God entered a real household.

In Isaiah the way is prepared for the LORD himself, Israel's God coming to his people. Applying the verse to the forerunner of Jesus identifies Jesus' coming with God's own coming, the same claim Matthew made in the name Immanuel (1:23).

“He was hungry” is one of the plainest statements of Jesus' full humanity in the Gospels. The Son of God is tested in a real body with real needs, which is why Hebrews can say he was made like his brothers in every way and is able to help those who are tempted (Hebrews 2:17-18).
If ‘Son of God’ is original here, the book opens and closes (15:39) with the same confession. Even without it, the prologue's voice from heaven (1:11) gives Jesus that identity.

By applying to Jesus a text about the coming of the LORD, Mark identifies Jesus' coming with the coming of Israel's God. This is one of the earliest and most striking ways the New Testament says who Jesus is.

The scribes' premise is sound: forgiveness of sins against God is God's prerogative (Isaiah 43:25). Mark does not correct the premise; he lets it stand so that the reader draws the conclusion about Jesus that the scribes refuse.

Jesus feels real anger and real grief, and both are directed at the same hardness. The verse shows the Son of God's full humanity, and it shows anger that is holy because it is joined to sorrow for the people who provoke it.

The same person sleeps from exhaustion and commands the storm. Mark puts the full humanity and the divine authority of Jesus side by side in two consecutive verses without explaining how they belong together, which is the question the church's confession of Christ as fully God and fully man later answered.

Jesus tells the man to report what ‘the Lord’ has done; the man reports what Jesus has done, and Mark lets both statements stand. The narrative identifies the work of Jesus with the work of Israel's God without comment.

Did Jesus not know who touched him, or did he ask in order to draw her out? John Chrysostom, preaching on Matthew's version (Homilies on Matthew 31), held that he knew and called her forward to free her from fear and to make her faith known. Many modern interpreters take the question at face value, seeing in it the real limits of knowledge the Son accepted in becoming human (compare Mark 13:32). Both readings confess him fully divine and fully human; they differ on how that union showed itself in this moment.

The Son of God had a trade, a mother, brothers and sisters with ordinary names, and neighbors who thought they knew all about him. The verse shows how completely he entered ordinary human life, so completely that those closest to it could not see past it.

Jesus does what Scripture says God alone does, walking on the waves, and names himself with words God uses of himself. Mark does not explain; he shows, and leaves the disciples and the reader to reckon with who this is.
The Son shares the limits of human knowledge in his earthly life. The church has confessed that he is truly God and truly man, and verses like this one guard the full reality of his humanity.

The church appealed to Gethsemane against any view in which Christ's humanity was only apparent. Jesus has a human soul (psuchē) that is ‘consumed with sorrow’, and the Council of Chalcedon (451) and later the Third Council of Constantinople (681), which affirmed a human will in Christ, drew on this scene.

The conception is God's creative act through the Spirit, without a human father and without any hint of a divine partner. The church confesses on this verse that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary (the Apostles' Creed).
The unborn Jesus, only days or weeks conceived, is already ‘my Lord’. The verse gives no stage of his human life in which he is less than who he is.

The Son of the Most High (1:32) is wrapped in cloths and laid in a feeding trough. Luke tells the incarnation not by explaining it but by the plainest details of a birth, the humility Paul describes in Philippians 2:6-8.
God's sign of the Messiah is his poverty. The mark by which he is recognized is the lowliness Mary sang of (1:48, 1:52).
The Son of God grows. Luke's description of a real childhood, with real development in wisdom, is part of the church's confession that Christ is truly human.
A twelve-year-old calls God his Father in a unique sense and says he ‘must’ be in his house. The verse shows the Son's awareness of his relation to the Father within a truly human childhood.
Luke says plainly that Jesus grew in wisdom. The church's confession that he is true God does not erase the verse; it affirms that he had a real human mind that learned.

‘As was supposed’ holds together two truths: Jesus was legally Joseph's son and heir, and he was not conceived by Joseph. The genealogy places the Son of God within a human family without denying his origin in God.
The objection states the premise that the rest of the scene answers: only God can forgive sins. Jesus does not deny it; he forgives. Luke lets the reader draw the conclusion the critics would not.
The Sabbath was God's own day (‘a Sabbath to the LORD your God’, Exodus 20:10). To call himself its Lord is to claim a place Israel's Scriptures reserve for God.

The Son of Man ‘came eating and drinking’. Jesus' mission is carried out through ordinary human table fellowship, eating with those whom others avoided, and that visible humanity became the ground of the charge against him.

The guests' question is the right one. In Israel's Scriptures forgiveness belongs to God (Psalm 130:4, Isaiah 43:25), and the scribes in 5:21 had already said so. Jesus pronounces forgiveness in his own voice, and Luke leaves the reader to draw the conclusion the guests could not.

The disciples' question is the right one. The one who falls asleep from tiredness is also the one whom wind and water obey; Luke shows full humanity and divine authority in the same boat, and leaves the reader to answer who he is.

Luke lets the two sentences stand together: Jesus says God has done it, and the man says Jesus did. The narrator does not correct him. What God does, Jesus does, and the witness who tells one is telling the other.

The Son of Man, the figure of Daniel 7 who receives glory and a kingdom, has less shelter than a fox. Luke's Jesus accepts homelessness on the road to Jerusalem, and the Samaritan refusal just narrated is a case in point. The glory of the mountain and the poverty of the road belong to the same person.

The one who speaks as a traveling teacher on the road to Jerusalem claims a relation to the Father that belongs to God alone. Luke sets this claim in the middle of a human scene of prayer and joy, the pattern the church confessed as one person, truly God and truly man.
The Son feels real distress as his death approaches. Luke does not present a Jesus untouched by fear, but one whose full humanity feels the weight of what he has come to do, as in Gethsemane (22:44).

The verse does not deny Christ's goodness or deity; it sets the question before the ruler. Read with the whole Gospel, where Jesus forgives sins, receives thanks as glory to God (17:15-18), and calls people to follow him in place of their possessions, the church hears in it an invitation to recognize God present in the teacher.

Paul summarizes the same double identity: descended from David according to the flesh, declared Son of God in power by the resurrection (Romans 1:3-4). The church's confession that Christ is truly human and truly God gave the full answer to Jesus' question, and Luke's infancy story, with its promise that the son of David would be called Son of God (1:32-35), points toward it.

The Son asks that the cup pass and then submits his will to the Father's. The church read the verse as evidence that the incarnate Son has a true human will, able to shrink from suffering, which he freely aligns with the divine will; a Christ without that human will could not pray this prayer.

If the verses are original, they show the Son's human nature under extreme strain, needing and receiving strength. Irenaeus used them against those who said Christ only seemed to have a body. Whatever one concludes about the text, the doctrine does not depend on them; Hebrews says the same of his prayers with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7).

The Son did not shed his humanity at the resurrection. His body remains human and wounded, which is why the church confesses that Christ ascended and reigns as a man, the one mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5).
The one who becomes flesh in verse 14 is introduced first as eternal. The incarnation in John is not a man raised to divine status but the Word who already was God taking on flesh.

The Word did not put on a disguise or come to live inside a man; he became flesh. The Council of Chalcedon (451) confessed one person in two natures, truly God and truly human, as a guard on exactly this sentence.

The Son of Man is the one who came down from heaven. The verse joins the title of Daniel 7 to the prologue's teaching that the Word came from God, so that the Son of Man is not merely a man raised up but one who first descended.

This is the only place in John where Jesus is said to be tired. The Gospel that begins with the Word who was God (1:1) shows him sitting down exhausted at noon and asking a stranger for water. The church confesses both natures in one person, and verses like this keep the humanity from being a disguise.

The tired and hungry man of verse 6 says that doing the Father's will sustains him. The Son's human life is lived entirely from the Father's will, the pattern of the obedience that culminates at the cross.

The earliest opponents understood Jesus' words as a claim to divine status, which is why they sought his death. The verse is important evidence that the high Christology of John is not a later softening misunderstanding but the point at issue in Jesus' conflicts.

The bread of God is a person who comes down from heaven. Verse 33 is the first of seven times in the chapter that Jesus' origin is described with ‘come down’, and it makes the incarnation the ground of the gift: life is given to the world because the Son has come into it.

The Son's coming down is a real descent with a purpose, and the purpose is obedience. The verse joins the incarnation to Jesus' submission to the Father, which the Gospels show in Gethsemane and which John voices in 4:34 and 5:30.

The objection states half the truth. Jesus is the son of a known family in Galilee, and he has come down from heaven. John has already told the reader both (1:14, 1:45), and the grumblers take the first as disproof of the second. The incarnation means both are true of the same person.

Jesus' challenge presupposes his sinlessness, which the rest of the New Testament confesses: he was tempted in every way yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), and he knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). The Word who became flesh took a full human life without its bondage to sin.
The man not yet fifty is the eternal Son. The verse holds together what the prologue said: the Word who was with God in the beginning (1:1) became flesh (1:14) without ceasing to be who he was.

The charge states the Christian confession in reverse. The accusers say he is a man who makes himself God; John's Gospel says he is God, the Word, who became a man (1:1, 14). The accusation is false not because Jesus is less than they fear but because the direction of his coming is the opposite of what they suppose.

The Son is the one the Father consecrated and sent into the world. The pairing of consecration and sending presupposes his existence with the Father before his coming, and at the feast of the temple's consecration it presents him as the one truly set apart for God.

The Son of God has a human spirit that can be stirred to indignation and distress. John, who has the highest view of Jesus' divinity in the Gospels, is also the one who shows most plainly that his emotions were real, not a performance.

The Word who became flesh (1:14) sheds human tears. Hebrews remembers the same Jesus offering prayers with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7): the one who shares the Father's glory also shares the grief of the people he came to save.

The Son who says he came for this hour also feels its horror. His obedience is not the calm of someone who feels nothing, but a human will choosing the Father's will through real distress (Hebrews 5:7-8).

The one who came from God and is returning to God kneels at his disciples' feet. John makes humility the expression of Jesus' divine identity rather than a veil over it, as Paul does in Philippians 2:6-8.
Jesus knows the betrayal is coming and has foretold it, yet he is troubled by it. Foreknowledge does not make him indifferent; betrayal by a friend wounds him as it would any person.

The longing to see God is answered in a human face. The verse does not say that Jesus resembles the Father or points to him, but that seeing him is seeing the Father, which is the incarnation stated in terms of sight: the Word who was God became flesh and was seen (1:14, 1 John 1:1-2).

The devil finds nothing in Jesus, no sin and no guilt, to which his accusation can hold. The New Testament's confession of the sinless Son (Hebrews 4:15, 1 Peter 2:22) has its Johannine form here and in Jesus' challenge in 8:46.

Jesus knows his disciples' hearts and meets their questions before they can put them into words. The Gospel presents this knowledge as one of the signs of who he is, without denying the real human limits it also records (11:34).

Jesus' origin is with the Father, and his coming into the world is a coming from God, not the rise of a human being to divine favor. The verse is a compact form of what the prologue says of the Word who was with God and became flesh (1:1, 1:14).

The one who asks to return to his former glory is the Son who laid it aside to finish his work on earth. The verse gives the shape of the incarnation from the inside: glory before the world, work on earth, glory again with the Father (Philippians 2:6-11).

In one sentence Jesus speaks of being born and of coming into the world. The pairing holds together what the Gospel says in 1:14: the eternal Word came from the Father and was truly born as a man, and his purpose in both is to make the truth known.

Pilate displays Jesus' humanity at its most wounded, and the Gospel that said the Word became flesh (1:14) lets the phrase stand as a confession it never intended. The Son of God is presented to the world as ‘the man’, fully human in weakness and shame.

The accusers state as a crime what the Gospel confesses as the truth: Jesus is the Son of God, not by self-promotion but because he came from the Father (5:19-23, 10:36). The charge that condemns him names the identity that saves.

Thomas confesses as God the one whose wounds he has just been invited to touch. The confession holds together what the prologue declared: the Word who was God became flesh (1:1, 1:14). The risen Jesus is fully human, bearing the marks of the cross, and he is Lord and God.

Peter's first description of Jesus is ‘a man’. The church's confession of Jesus' deity, which the sermon reaches in verses 34-36, never removes the plain fact of his humanity that the first witnesses knew.

The Son is called God's Son before the clause about David, so the verse assumes his sonship precedes his human birth. He ‘came to be’ from David's line; he did not begin to be. Philippians 2:6-8 and Galatians 4:4 draw the same line.
Jesus Christ is ‘the one man’ set beside Adam. His true humanity is essential to Paul's argument: a new head of humanity must be human, yet the grace that flows from him is ‘the grace of God’.

‘In the likeness of sinful man’ holds together the two truths the church later confessed at Chalcedon (451): the Son took real human nature, weak and mortal, and remained without sin. ‘His own Son’ implies that he was the Son before he was sent.

‘According to the flesh’ places the Messiah's human descent in Israel. If the clause that follows refers to Christ, the verse states both natures in one sentence: descended from the patriarchs as man, and God over all. That is how almost all the church fathers read it, including Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Origen.

The verse speaks of Christ's existence in the form of God before he took the form of a servant. The church's confession that the Son existed before his human birth and chose to become human draws directly on this verse, whatever the precise sense of harpagmos.

The church's reading of the emptying within the faith of Chalcedon (AD 451) holds that the Son took human nature without losing or changing his divine nature. Augustine put it in On the Trinity (book 1) that he took the form of a servant without losing the form of God, and Pope Leo's Tome (449) described the emptying as a stooping down in compassion, not a failure of power. Nineteenth century kenotic theologians, beginning with Gottfried Thomasius in Germany, proposed that the Son laid aside certain divine attributes; the chapter note sets out that debate.
God's whole fullness dwells in Christ, and 2:9 adds ‘bodily’. There is no part of God lacking in him and no need to seek divine fullness through other powers or practices.
The Son took real flesh and blood, entering the human condition he had not shared before. The purpose of the incarnation was death, and through death, victory.
The Son's experience of testing was real. The church has confessed both that he was truly tempted and that he did not sin (4:15), holding together his genuine humanity and his holiness.

Jesus' testing was real because his humanity was real. Gregory of Nazianzus (Letter 101) argued against Apollinarius that what the Son did not assume he did not heal, so he took a complete human nature, including a human mind and will; this verse is part of the biblical ground for that conviction.

‘The days of his flesh’ names the whole span of the Son's earthly life in the vulnerability of human nature. The verse forbids any picture of Christ's humanity as a costume; he feared death and cried out to the Father.

The eternal Son did not cease to be Son, yet in his human nature he grew in the experience of obedience (compare Luke 2:52). The church's confession at Chalcedon (451) that Christ is fully God and fully human makes room for exactly this: real human learning in one who is truly the Son.

The Son's coming into the world is described as God preparing a body for him. The incarnation is the means of the atonement: the obedience God desired had to be offered in a human body, and the Son took one for that purpose.
